title: Chapter 41. Of the Office of Our Blessed Saviour
section: Part III — Of a Christian Commonwealth
paragraphs: We find in Holy Scripture three parts of the office of the Messiah. The first, of a Redeemer, or Saviour. The second, of a Pastor, Counsellor, or Teacher — that is, of a prophet sent from God to convert such as God has elected to salvation. The third, of a King, and Eternal King, but under his Father — as Moses and the high priests were in their several times. And to these three parts correspond three times. Our redemption he wrought at his first coming, by the sacrifice in which he offered up himself for our sins on the cross. Our conversion he wrought partly then in his own person, and partly works now by his ministers, and will continue to work till his coming again. And after his coming again shall begin that glorious reign of his over his elect, which is to last eternally.

To the office of a Redeemer — that is, of one who pays the ransom of sin (which ransom is death) — it belongs that he was sacrificed, and thereby bore on his own head, and carried away from us, our iniquities, in such a way as God had required. Not that the death of one man, though without sin, can satisfy for the offences of all men, in the rigour of justice; but in the mercy of God, who ordained such sacrifices for sin as he was pleased in his mercy to accept. In the old law (as we may read in Leviticus 16), the Lord required that every year there should be made an atonement for the sins of all Israel, both priests and others. To do this, Aaron alone was to sacrifice, for himself and the priests, a young bullock; and for the rest of the people, he was to receive from them two young goats, of which he was to sacrifice one; but as for the other, which was the scapegoat, he was to lay his hands on its head, and by a confession of the iniquities of the people, to lay them all on that head, and then, by some convenient man, to cause the goat to be led into the wilderness, and there to escape, and carry away with it the iniquities of the people. As the sacrifice of the one goat was a sufficient (because an acceptable) price for the ransom of all Israel, so the death of the Messiah is a sufficient price for the sins of all mankind, because there was no more required. Our Saviour Christ's sufferings seem to be figured here as clearly as in the oblation of Isaac, or in any other type of him in the Old Testament. He was both the sacrificed goat and the scapegoat. 'He was oppressed, and he was afflicted,' (Isa. 53:7), 'he opened not his mouth; he was brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep is dumb before the shearer, so opened he not his mouth' — here he is the sacrificed goat. 'He has borne our griefs (verse 4), and carried our sorrows'; and again (verse 6), 'the Lord has laid on him the iniquities of us all' — and so he is the scapegoat. 'He was cut off from the land of the living (verse 8), for the transgression of my people' — there again he is the sacrificed goat. And again (verse 11), 'he shall bear their sins' — he is the scapegoat. So the Lamb of God is equivalent to both those goats: sacrificed, in that he died; and escaping, in his resurrection — being raised conveniently by his Father, and removed from the habitation of men in his ascension.

Inasmuch, therefore, as the one who redeems has no title to the thing redeemed before the redemption and ransom is paid, and this ransom was the death of the Redeemer, it is plain that our Saviour (as man) was not king of those he redeemed before he suffered death — that is, during the time he conversed bodily on the earth. I say, he was not then king in present, by virtue of the pact which the faithful make with him in baptism; nevertheless, by the renewing of their pact with God in baptism, they were obliged to obey him for king (under his Father), whenever he should be pleased to take the kingdom upon him. According to this, our Saviour himself expressly says (John 18:36), 'My kingdom is not of this world.' Now since Scripture makes mention of only two worlds — this one that is now, and shall remain until the day of judgement (which is therefore also called the last day), and that which shall be a new heaven and a new earth — the kingdom of Christ is not to begin till the general resurrection. And this is what our Saviour says (Matt. 16:27): 'The Son of man shall come in the glory of his Father, with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.' To reward every man according to his works is to execute the office of a king; and this is not to be until he comes in the glory of his Father, with his angels. When our Saviour says (Matt. 23:2), 'The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses's seat; all therefore that they bid you do, observe and do,' he plainly declares that he ascribes kingly power, for that time, not to himself but to them. And so he does also where he says (Luke 12:14), 'Who made me a judge, or divider, over you?' And (John 12:47), 'I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.' And yet our Saviour came into this world that he might be a king and a judge in the world to come; for he was the Messiah, that is, the Christ, that is, the Anointed Priest, and the Sovereign Prophet of God — that is, he was to have all the power that was in Moses the prophet, in the high priests who succeeded Moses, and in the kings who succeeded the priests. And St John says expressly (chapter 5, verse 22), 'The Father judges no man, but has committed all judgement to the Son.' And this is not repugnant to that other passage, 'I came not to judge the world,' for this is spoken of the present world, the other of the world to come; as also where it is said that at the second coming of Christ (Matt. 19:28), 'You that have followed me in the regeneration, when the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his glory, you shall also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.'
The end of Christ's coming was to renew the covenant of the kingdom of God, and to persuade the elect to embrace it — which was the second part of his office.

If, then, Christ while he was on earth had no kingdom in this world, to what end was his first coming? It was to restore to God, by a new covenant, the kingdom which, being his by the old covenant, had been cut off by the rebellion of the Israelites in the election of Saul. To do this, he was to preach to them that he was the Messiah — that is, the king promised to them by the prophets; and to offer himself in sacrifice for the sins of those who should by faith submit themselves to him; and, in case the nation generally should reject him, to call to his obedience such as should believe in him among the Gentiles. So there are two parts of our Saviour's office during his sojourn upon the earth: one, to proclaim himself the Christ; and another, by teaching and by working miracles, to persuade and to prepare men to live in such a way as to be worthy of the immortality believers were to enjoy at such time as he should come in majesty to take possession of his Father's kingdom. And so it is that the time of his preaching is often called by himself the regeneration; which is not properly a kingdom — and thereby a warrant to deny obedience to the magistrates that then were (for he commanded men to obey those who then sat in Moses's chair, and to pay tribute to Caesar) — but only an earnest of the kingdom of God that was to come, to those to whom God had given the grace to be his disciples, and to believe in him. For which cause the godly are said to be already in the kingdom of grace, as naturalised in that heavenly kingdom.

Up to this point, then, there is nothing done, or taught, by Christ that tends to the diminution of the civil right of the Jews, or of Caesar. For as touching the commonwealth that then was among the Jews, both those who bore rule among them and those who were governed all expected the Messiah, and the kingdom of God; which they could not have done if their laws had forbidden him (when he came) to manifest, and declare, himself. Since therefore he did nothing but, by preaching and miracles, go about to prove himself to be that Messiah, he did nothing in this against their laws. The kingdom he claimed was to be in another world; he taught all men to obey, in the meantime, those who sat in Moses's seat; he allowed them to give Caesar his tribute, and refused to take upon himself the role of a judge. How then could his words, or actions, be seditious, or tend to the overthrow of their then civil government? But God, having determined his sacrifice for the reduction of his elect to their former covenanted obedience, used their malice and ingratitude as the means by which he would bring this to effect. Nor was it contrary to the laws of Caesar. For though Pilate himself (to gratify the Jews) delivered him to be crucified, yet before he did so he pronounced openly that he found no fault in him; and put as the title of his condemnation, not (as the Jews required) 'that he claimed to be king,' but simply 'That he was king of the Jews'; and notwithstanding their clamour, refused to alter it, saying, 'What I have written, I have written.'

As for the third part of his office, which was to be king, I have already shown that his kingdom was not to begin until the resurrection. But then he shall be king, not only as God (in which sense he is king already, and ever shall be, of all the earth, by virtue of his omnipotence), but also peculiarly of his own elect, by virtue of the pact they make with him in their baptism. And it is therefore that our Saviour says (Matt. 19:28) that his apostles should sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel, 'When the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his glory' — whereby he signified that he should reign then in his human nature. And (Matt. 16:27), 'The Son of man shall come in the glory of his Father, with his angels, and then he shall reward every man according to his works.' The same we may read in Mark 13:26 and 14:26; and more expressly for the time, in Luke 22:29–30: 'I appoint to you a kingdom, as my Father has appointed to me, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.' By which it is plain that the kingdom of Christ appointed to him by his Father is not to be before the Son of man shall come in glory, and make his apostles judges of the twelve tribes of Israel. But a man may here ask: seeing there is no marriage in the kingdom of heaven, whether men shall then eat and drink — and what eating, therefore, is meant in this passage? This is explained by our Saviour (John 6:27), where he says: 'Labour not for the meat that perishes, but for that meat that endures to everlasting life, which the Son of man shall give you.' So by 'eating at Christ's table' is meant the eating of the tree of life — that is, the enjoyment of immortality, in the kingdom of the Son of man. By these passages, and many more, it is plain that our Saviour's kingdom is to be exercised by him in his human nature.

Again, he is to be king then, no otherwise than as subordinate, or vice-regent, of God the Father — as Moses was in the wilderness, and as the high priests were before the reign of Saul, and as the kings were after it. For it is one of the prophecies concerning Christ that he should be like Moses (in office): 'I will raise them up a prophet (says the Lord, Deut. 18:18) from among their brethren like you, and will put my words into his mouth.' And this similarity with Moses is also apparent in the actions of our Saviour himself, while he was on earth. For as Moses chose twelve princes of the tribes to govern under him, so did our Saviour choose twelve apostles, who shall sit on twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel; and as Moses authorised seventy elders to receive the Spirit of God, and to prophesy to the people — that is (as I said before), to speak to them in the name of God — so our Saviour also ordained seventy disciples to preach his kingdom, and salvation, to all nations. And as when a complaint was made to Moses against those of the seventy who prophesied in the camp of Israel, he justified them in it as being subservient in this to his government, so also our Saviour, when St John complained to him of a certain man who cast out devils in his name, justified him in it, saying (Luke 9:50), 'Forbid him not, for he who is not against us is on our side.'

Again, our Saviour resembled Moses in the institution of sacraments — both of admission into the kingdom of God, and of commemoration of his deliverance of his elect from their miserable condition. As the children of Israel had for sacrament of their reception into the kingdom of God, before the time of Moses, the rite of circumcision (which rite, having been omitted in the wilderness, was again restored as soon as they came into the land of promise), so also the Jews, before the coming of our Saviour, had a rite of baptising — that is, of washing with water all those who, being Gentiles, embraced the God of Israel. This rite St John the Baptist used in the receiving of all those who gave in their names to the Christ, whom he preached as already come into the world; and our Saviour instituted the same for a sacrament to be taken by all who believed in him. From what cause the rite of baptism first proceeded is not expressed formally in the Scripture; but it may probably be thought to be an imitation of the law of Moses concerning leprosy, in which the leper was commanded to be kept out of the camp of Israel for a certain time, after which time, being judged by the priest to be clean, he was admitted into the camp after a solemn washing. And this may therefore be a type of the washing in baptism, in which men who are cleansed of the leprosy of sin by faith are received into the church with the solemnity of baptism. There is another conjecture drawn from the ceremonies of the Gentiles, in a certain case that rarely happens — namely, when a man who was thought dead happened to recover, other men made scruple to converse with him, as they would to converse with a ghost, unless he were received again into the number of men by washing, as children newly born were washed from the uncleanness of their nativity (which was a kind of new birth). This ceremony of the Greeks, in the time that Judea was under the dominion of Alexander, and the Greeks his successors, may probably enough have crept into the religion of the Jews. But since it is not likely our Saviour would countenance a heathen rite, it is most likely it proceeded from the legal ceremony of washing after leprosy. And for the other sacrament, of eating the paschal lamb, it is plainly imitated in the sacrament of the Lord's Supper, in which the breaking of the bread and the pouring out of the wine keep in memory our deliverance from the misery of sin by Christ's passion — as the eating of the paschal lamb kept in memory the deliverance of the Jews out of the bondage of Egypt. Since therefore the authority of Moses was but subordinate, and he but a lieutenant to God, it follows that Christ, whose authority, as man, was to be like that of Moses, was no more than subordinate to the authority of his Father. The same is more expressly signified by his teaching us to pray, 'Our Father, your kingdom come,' and 'for yours is the kingdom, the power, and the glory'; and by that it is said that 'He shall come in the glory of his Father'; and by what St Paul says (1 Cor. 15:24): 'then comes the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father'; and by many other most express passages.

Our Saviour therefore, both in teaching and in reigning, represents (as Moses did) the person of God — which God, from that time forward (but not before), is called the Father; and being still one and the same substance, is one person as represented by Moses, and another person as represented by his Son the Christ. For 'person' being a relative to a representer, it is consequent to a plurality of representers that there be a plurality of persons, even of one and the same substance.
